questions.question: 77712. Recovery from propofol anaesthesia is generally –
questions.explain: One of propofol's key advantages is quick and clear recovery with minimal residual sedation ("hangover" effect), making it popular for day-care/outpatient procedures.

questions.question: 77711. Which maternal viral infection in the first trimester is linked with increased cleft risk?
questions.explain: Maternal rubella infection during the first trimester is a recognized infective etiological factor.

questions.question: 77710. Primary objective of pre-prosthetic surgery is to.
questions.option4: Provide a favourable Foundation for Prosthesis
questions.explain: Pre-prosthetic surgery prepares the oral tissues for successful prosthetic rehabilitation.

questions.question: 77709. The philtrum of the upper lip, premaxilla, and primary palate are all derived from the –
questions.explain: The two medial nasal processes fuse in the midline to form the philtrum of the lip, premaxilla, primary palate, and nasal septum — this is distinct from the maxillary processes, which form the cheeks, lateral upper lip, and secondary palate.

questions.question: 77708. Bilateral cleft lip occur from-
questions.option1: Lack of Fusion Between maxillary process & lateral nasal process
questions.option2: Lack of fusion Between two medial process
questions.option3: Lack of fusion Between maxillary process & median nasal process
questions.option4: Failure of Mandibular & maxillary process to fuse
questions.explain:
Lack of Fusion Between maxillary process & lateral nasal process- oblique facial cleft
Lack of fusion Between two medial process - median cleft lip
Lack of fusion Between maxillary process & median nasal process-bilateral cleft lip
Failure of Mandibular & maxillary process to fuse

questions.question: 77707. Amide type of LA metabolized in-
questions.explain:
Amides are heat stable and safe, very rarely cause allergic reactions. Therefore, amides are now more commonly used than esters.

Metabolized in liver and excreted by the kidneys. They are mild vasodilators, therefore, end up with increased rate of absorption into the bloodstream

questions.question: 77706. "Frenectomy" differs from "frenotomy" primarily in that frenectomy involves –
questions.option1: simple incision/release of the frenum, commonly performed in infants
questions.option2: Complete surgical excision of the frenum along with its periosteal attachment
questions.option3: Treatment exclusively of the lingual frenum
questions.option4: It is indicated for only tongue tie
questions.explain: Frenectomy is a complete excision of the frenum plus its attachment to the underlying periosteum (indicated for high frenal attachment, midline diastema, ankyloglossia, or gingival recession), whereas frenotomy is a simple incision/release, typically done in infants for tongue-tie without complete removal.

questions.question: 77705. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for a NEWBORN infant with significant breastfeeding difficulty due to ankyloglossia?
questions.explain: In infants, a simple frenotomy is typically the preferred, minimally invasive first-line treatment to quickly improve tongue mobility and breastfeeding ability, avoiding the need for more extensive surgery.

questions.question: 77704. Widely used surface anesthesia in dentistry?
questions.explain: Benzocaine is widely used as surface anesthesia.

questions.question: 77703. Which drug combination classically produces "neurolept analgesia"?
questions.explain: Explanation: Neurolept analgesia is a state of profound analgesia and psychic indifference produced by combining a neuroleptic/butyrophenone (droperidol) with a potent opioid analgesic (fentanyl), without necessarily causing full unconsciousness.

questions.question: 77702. Alveoloplasty" is best defined as –
questions.option1: Complete surgical removal of a portion of the alveolar process
questions.option2: Recontouring and smoothing of the alveolar bone, typically after extraction
questions.option3: Excision of hyperplastic (flabby) soft tissue over the ridge
questions.option4: Bone grafting of a severely resorbed ridge
questions.explain: Alveoloplasty refers to recontouring/smoothing of alveolar bone after tooth extraction (simple, radical/Dean's, or intraseptal technique) — distinct from alveolectomy (B option A is closer to alveolectomy), soft tissue excision, or bone grafting/augmentation.

questions.question: 77701. An autoclave works on the principle of –
questions.explain: An autoclave sterilizes using saturated steam under pressure, which raises the boiling point of water above 100°C, allowing higher effective sterilizing temperatures than boiling at atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: 77700. Which infection can be prevented effectively By Vaccination among the dental professionals?
questions.explain: Hepatitis B vaccination provides effective protection against Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, which is a major occupational hazard for dental professionals due to frequent exposure to blood and body fluids.

questions.question: 77699. Trismus following an inferior alveolar nerve block injection most commonly results from –
questions.option1: Injury to the muscles of mastication
questions.explain: Trismus after IAN block is usually due to trauma to the muscles of mastication (commonly the medial pterygoid) from repeated needle insertions, hematoma formation, or low-grade infection — restricting mouth opening.

questions.question: 77698. Endodontic files, reamers, and broaches are most rapidly sterilized (in 5–15 seconds) using which chairside method?
questions.explain: The Glass Bead Sterilizer uses glass beads (or table salt substitute) heated to approximately 260°C (437–465°F), sterilizing small endodontic instruments in just 5–15 seconds — though the handle portion of the instrument remains unsterilized, which is a recognized limitation.

questions.question: 77697. Which of the following  is least toxic LA-
questions.explain: Toxicity of bupivacaine is less than four times that of lidocaine & mepivacaine. Propoxycaine is most toxic of all known LA's.

questions.question: 77696. The absolute contraindication among the following for administration of local anaesthesia is –
questions.option2: Myocardial infarction within the preceding 6 months
questions.explain: Recent MI (<6 months) is an absolute contraindication due to high cardiac instability risk. Renal failure, hypertension, and first-trimester pregnancy are relative contraindications requiring caution/modification rather than absolute avoidance.

questions.question: 77695. Which of the following is ultra-short acting LA-
questions.explain:

Procaine without a vasoconstrictor

2-chloroprocaine (1.2% or 3%) without a vaso-constrictor

2% lidocaine without a vasoconstrictor

4% prilocaine without a vasoconstrictor for infiltra-tion

questions.question: 77690. Which of the following maternal anticonvulsant drugs is a known teratogen associated with cleft lip/palate?
questions.explain: Maternal use of anticonvulsant drugs, particularly phenytoin, along with corticosteroids and retinoic acid, are recognized environmental/teratogenic risk factors for facial clefting.

questions.question: 77689. The lingual nerve, anaesthetised during an IAN block, supplies all of the following EXCEPT –
questions.option1: Anterior two-thirds of the tongue mucosa
questions.explain: The lingual nerve supplies the anterior 2/3rd tongue mucosa, floor of mouth, lingual gingiva, and sublingual/submandibular glands. The skin of the chin is supplied by the mental nerve (a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve), not the lingual nerve.

questions.question: 77688. Primary surgery intervention of lip done in....
questions.explain:

questions.question: 77687. Addition of a vasoconstrictor to local anaesthetic solution primarily results in –
questions.option3: Reduced rate of absorption and increased safety margin
questions.explain: Vasoconstriction at the injection site slows systemic uptake of the LA, keeping blood levels lower for longer, which both prolongs local anaesthesia and raises the safety margin against systemic toxicity — provided there is no accidental intravascular injection.

questions.question: 77686. The primary mechanism of action of local anaesthetics is –
questions.explain: LA molecules diffuse into the nerve, bind the sodium channel receptor site, and block sodium influx. This prevents the nerve membrane from depolarizing and reaching threshold potential, so no propagated action potential (and hence no conduction) occurs. Potassium conductance is largely unaffected, ruling out A and D. Calcium's role is only in the initial displacement step, not the final blockade mechanism (C).

questions.option2: Removal of redundant crestal flabby soft tissue
questions.explain:

Soft tissue surgeries

questions.question: 77683. Fine, scattered radiopaque foci ("snowflake calcifications") within a pericoronal radiolucency are classically suggestive of:
questions.explain: Appears as a well-circumscribed pericoronal radiolucency (mimicking a dentigerous cyst) that characteristically extends beyond the cementoenamel junction (often down the root) and contains classic "snowflake" calcifications.

questions.question: 77682. The most common benign tumor-like lesion of the maxillary antrum lining is:
questions.explain: Antral (antrochoanal) polyps arise from hyperplastic mucosal lining, often secondary to chronic sinusitis or allergy.

questions.question: 77681. Ghost cells on histology are diagnostic of:
questions.explain: Ghost cells (aberrant keratinisation of epithelial cells that lose their nuclei but retain the cell outline) are the histological hallmark of the calcifying odontogenic cyst, along with ameloblast-like basal cells.

questions.question: 77680. Root resorption caused by ameloblastoma classically has which appearance, distinguishing it from resorption due to simple pressure from a cyst?
questions.option3: Complete disappearance of the root with no radiographic change
questions.explain: Ameloblastoma tends to produce a jagged, irregular, "nibbled"/knife-edge pattern of root resorption due to its locally infiltrative growth, in contrast to the smoother, more rounded resorption typically caused by the gradual pressure effect of a benign cyst.

questions.question: 77679. A common nutritional deficiency associated with recurrent aphthous ulcers is:
questions.explain: Deficiencies of B12, folate, and iron are well-documented hematinic deficiencies linked to increased frequency/severity of RAS; correction of these deficiencies often reduces recurrence.

questions.question: 77678. The most common type of recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) is:
questions.explain: Minor aphthous ulcer (Mikulicz's ulcer) accounts for ~80-85% of all RAS cases, presenting as small (<1cm), shallow ulcers that heal without scarring in 7-14 days.

questions.question: 77677. The articular surface of the TMJ is covered by:
questions.explain: Unlike most synovial joints (which have hyaline cartilage), the TMJ is lined by fibrocartilage — better suited to withstand mechanical stress and has superior repair capacity.

questions.question: 77676. Which of the following is the true functional ligament of the TMJ?
questions.explain: The temporomandibular ligament (lateral ligament) is the only ligament directly attached to the joint capsule and actively controls/limits mandibular movements. The sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments are accessory ligaments that support but don't functionally guide the joint.

questions.question: 77675. The main clinical hallmark that distinguishes OSF from other potentially malignant disorders is:
questions.option4: Progressive fibrosis causing limitation of mouth opening
questions.explain: OSF is characterized by the oral mucosa becoming fibrotic, immobile, and progressively contracting — causing limitation of mouth opening (trismus) — a distinguishing clinical feature not typically seen in leukoplakia or erythroplakia alone.

questions.question: 77674. Advantages of enucleation over marsupialization of a jaw cyst include:
questions.option1: Slow shrinkage allowing preservation of adjacent teeth
questions.option2: Complete lining available for histological examination and treatment finished in one episode
questions.option3: Reduced risk of mandibular fracture in very large cysts
questions.option4: No aftercare required regardless of cyst
questions.explain: Enucleation removes the entire cyst lining in one procedure, allowing complete histological examination and heals without further follow-up in most cases — though it carries risks such as haemorrhage, nerve damage, or fracture in very large lesions (where marsupialization may be preferred first).

questions.question: 77673. Which is the most common mesenchymal (connective tissue) malignancy of the oral cavity?
questions.explain: Among the malignant connective tissue (mesenchymal) neoplasms of the oral cavity — which also include fibrosarcoma, liposarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, and lymphoma — Kaposi's sarcoma is specifically noted as the most common type of intra-oral sarcoma. It is an AIDS-defining illness in HIV-positive patients, caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), arising from microvascular endothelial tissue. It presents as painless, flat pigmented macules on the palate/gingiva that enlarge, become raised, and may eventually ulcerate.

questions.question: 77672. Which type of oral ulcer is preceded by vesicles/bullae?
questions.explain: Primary herpetic stomatitis (like herpes labialis, herpes zoster/chickenpox, and hand-foot-mouth disease) begins as vesicles/bullae that rupture to form ulcers, unlike aphthous, traumatic, or tuberculous ulcers, which arise without preceding vesiculation.

questions.question: 77671. Which cyst's fluid characteristically shows a dirty, creamy-white viscous suspension with low protein content (<5 g/100 ml)?
questions.explain: Aspirate of OKC is a dirty white/creamy viscous suspension of parakeratinised squamous cells, and its protein content is characteristically low (below 5 g/100 ml, often <4 g/100 ml albumin) — a useful diagnostic differentiator from other cysts.

questions.question: 77670. Odontogenic tumours are best managed by:
questions.explain: Odontogenic tumours (benign but sometimes locally aggressive, e.g. ameloblastoma) are managed surgically — excision, enucleation, or resection depending on type — rather than radiotherapy or chemotherapy, which are largely ineffective.

questions.question: 77669. Odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) is believed to develop from remnants of which embryological structure?
questions.explain:
OKC arises from remnants of the dental lamina.
These remnants are also called rests of Serres.
The lesion has an aggressive growth pattern.
Recurrence is common after treatment.

questions.option3: Reduced enamel epithelium and the crown of an unerupted tooth

Reduced enamel epithelium and the crown of an unerupted toothExplanation:Fluid accumulates around the crown of an impacted tooth.

questions.question: 77666. Which site is most frequently affected by oral squamous cell carcinoma?
questions.explain:
Lateral border of the tongue is a high-risk site for oral cancer.
Thin mucosa allows carcinogen penetration.
Lesions are often painless initially.
Biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

questions.question: 77665. Which odontogenic tumor most commonly occurs in the posterior mandible of adults aged 30–60 years?
questions.explain:
It usually affects middle-aged adults.
The posterior mandible is the commonest site.
It grows slowly but is locally invasive.

questions.question: 77664. An oral ulcer that persists for more than two weeks without healing should always raise suspicion of which condition?
questions.explain:
Persistent ulcers require biopsy.
SCC commonly presents as a non-healing ulcer.
Early diagnosis improves survival.
Tobacco is the major risk factor.

questions.question: 77663. The most common cyst of the jaw overall is:
questions.explain: Because dental caries is such a common etiologic factor, radicular cyst has the highest overall prevalence among jaw cysts.
